newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein M.P.'s to London to protest office ban.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein M.P.'s to London to protest office ban.

text.p: The leaders of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, travel to London on Monday to protest against a ban on them using offices in Britain's parliament, to which they were elected on May 1.
"We will be at Westminister to secure our entitlement as elected representatives," Martin McGuinness, the party's chief negotiator told Sky Television.

Last week he and party President Gerry Adams were banned from using offices and other facilities in Britain's Westminister parliament because they refused to take the oath of allegiance to the Queen which every incoming legislator must.

Their party, and its Irish Republican Army (IRA) sympathisers, want an end to British rule of Northern Ireland and the reunification of the province with the Irish republic, while a Protestant majority want it to remain British.
Adams refused to say at the weekend whether his party would take legal action to try to secure offices, free telephones and other facilities to which the 659 legislators are entitled.
But McGuinness said the showdown might "put the British people in a situation where they are exposed throughout the world."
The visit was aimed at "explaining to the British people that we are entitled to be supported so that our people (voters) will not be disadvantaged or discriminated against."
Adams argued at the weekend that his party had no other place to send elected representatives even though it was to a parliament whose authority over Northern Ireland it contests.

He accused the Speaker of the parliament, Betty Boothroyd, who took the decision to ban Sinn Fein, of changing the rules. "It's a case of one day Britannia rules the waves and next day Britannia waves the rules," he said.

The one-day London visit will take place amid moves by the new Labour government to hold preliminary talks with Sinn Fein, ending months of international isolation to punish the IRA for ending a 17-month ceasefire in February last year.

The initiative, announced in Belfast by Prime Minister Tony Blair on Friday, has met a lukewarm response from Sinn Fein, which says the ban was wrong in the first place and maintains that the IRA is a separate organisation.

The London visit will be part of a campaign by Sinn Fein to demand its inclusion at Belfast peace talks from which it has been banned since the start last year because of the IRA's failure to end its war against British rule.

McGuinness gave no hint of a new IRA ceasefire but said he wanted the talks to take place against a "peaceful background". The IRA has not carried out any attacks in Northern Ireland since a sniper seriously wounded a policewoman last month.

He said Sinn Fein wanted assurances from Blair's government that the talks would have a six to nine-month time frame, be meaningful and credible and would not turn into negotiations to make the IRA surrender its arsenals.
"We need to know that decommissioning is not going to be a blockage to substantive negotiations," McGuinness said.

The British government and pro-British Unionists in the province, who want it to remain British, argued that Sinn Fein cannot be admitted while its armed supporters could wreck or challenge any settlement it disapproved of.
The previous government said decommissioning could be tackled in parallel with talks on the province's future but insisted that the IRA had to prove a commitment to democracy.
